description: REGION BOUNDARY AS A SUBGRAPH, not a label field. `vision_motion_group` establishes which cells group together by DIFFUSING a label (`mo_flood`), which needs one pass per hop and represents membership as equality of a number. This seed derives the same partition's BOUNDARY instead, from the same pairwise predicate, with no diffusion at all: an edge disagrees or it does not, and that is decidable locally in one pass. The rim of a region is then an ordinary subgraph -- `rim_next` edges between adjacent boundary cells of the same region -- which a reader traverses to emit a contour. A contour is a path, and a path is what StrokeQuantize turns into a held shape; a label is recognisable as nothing. Reuses the field's own tolerance (`mtol`, broadcast by mo_tol_broadcast) -- no new threshold enters here.

rules.name: bt_disagree
rules.comment: A `neighbour` pair whose motion vectors differ by MORE than the field's own tolerance is a boundary crossing. Purely pairwise: no closure, no diffusion, and the same Magnitude(VecSub(...)) mo_pair_diff already computes. Fires once per crossing -- the edge insert is idempotent, so a settled field reports no progress.

rules.name: bt_boundary_cell
rules.comment: A cell on the rim: it has at least one crossing. Marked as an attribute so later rules can match rim-to-rim without re-deriving the predicate.

rules.name: bt_border_rim
rules.comment: THE FIELD EDGE IS A BOUNDARY TOO. `bt_disagree` can only mark a crossing where a `neighbour` edge EXISTS, so a region running off the edge of the field had an OPEN rim -- measured: the three parallax regions traced as straight vertical lines with zero width, whose quantized signatures then matched each other vacuously. A cell on the field's own perimeter is on the rim by construction. The extent comes from the field's H/W, never a constant here.

rules.name: bt_rim_link
rules.comment: Chain the rim. Two ADJACENT cells that are both on the rim and that AGREE with each other are consecutive on the same region's boundary, so they are linked. Following `rim_next` is a read-time traversal -- the contour exists as a path in the graph, not as a number replicated across an interior.

rules.name: bt_mint_crossing
rules.comment: THE BOUNDARY IS BETWEEN CELLS, SO REIFY IT AS A NODE. A `cuts` edge says two cells disagree; the BOUNDARY is the thing between them, and until it is a node it cannot be chained, addressed, or carried. Measured motivation: approximating the boundary by the CELLS beside it gave 140 rim cells for 60 crossings, and the rim was not a curve -- 25 cells of degree < 2, because a boundary turns DIAGONALLY while `neighbour` is 4-connected and no 4-connected edge can chain a staircase step. A crossing has no such problem: it is one object per disagreement. `cuts` is symmetric (the predicate is), so the pair would mint twice; the `Lt(R.cid, n.cid)` guard makes ONE of the two orderings canonical, and `add_node_if_absent` keyed on (lo, hi) makes the mint idempotent under re-firing.  SUCCESSOR IS NOT BUILT HERE, and the reason is measured. The obvious rule -- two crossings that share a CELL are consecutive -- was written, run, and removed: it yields 20% degree-2 against the rim-cell version's 81%, because 84 of the 98 boundary cells carry exactly ONE crossing. A cell on a straight boundary has one disagreeing neighbour, so consecutive cracks along it sit between DIFFERENT pairs of cells and share no cell. They share a CORNER. Expressing that needs the lattice vertex reified too, which needs coordinate arithmetic this seed deliberately does not carry -- so the successor relation is named and left unbuilt rather than approximated by a convention.

rules.name: bt_chain_collinear
rules.comment: CONSECUTIVE CRACKS ALONG A STRAIGHT BOUNDARY, with no coordinates. Measured: 84 of the 98 boundary cells carry exactly ONE crossing, so consecutive cracks there lie between DIFFERENT pairs of cells and share no cell -- which is why the share-a-cell rule alone scored 20% degree-2 and was removed. Two collinear cracks x=(A|B) and y=(C|D) are consecutive exactly when the cells correspond across them: A adjacent to C AND B adjacent to D. That is pure adjacency -- no lattice index, no doubled grid, no bare 2, and no angle sort. The corner they share is IMPLIED by the correspondence rather than reified.

rules.name: bt_chain_perpendicular
rules.comment: CRACKS THAT TURN A CORNER share the cell they turn around -- but only when they sit on ADJACENT sides of it. Linking every pair at a shared cell also links the two on OPPOSITE sides, which is a chord straight across the rim rather than a rim step. Measured: a rasterised circle came out with 8 of 100 boundary crossings at degree 3, and a contour walk took the chord and closed a loop half the figure's size (bbox 12x13 for a radius-12 circle). Adjacency of the two sides is stated without coordinates: the OTHER two cells are diagonal to each other exactly when they share a second common neighbour `m` besides the shared cell `c` -- the fourth corner of the 2x2 block. Cells on opposite sides of `c` share only `c`.

rules.name: bt_own
rules.comment:
BORDER OWNERSHIP, LOCALLY. `vision_border_ownership`'s bo_own gives a directed boundary that owns its figure -- the one thing the crossing construction lacked -- but reaches it through bo_bgflood, surroundedness as inward reachability from the frame, which costs a pass per hop. A crossing already holds both cells, so where figure and ground differ in magnitude the ownership is decidable AT THE CROSSING: the owned side is the stronger one. Measured on discs, an annulus and two discs, orienting each boundary cycle by this ownership makes its total turning +2pi for a figure and -2pi for a hole, every case correct, with no flood and no cell components.

THE LIMIT IS DELIBERATE AND IS WHERE bo_bgflood EARNS ITS COST. Ownership is CONTEXTUAL in the case that seed is built on -- Zhou/Friedman/von der Heydt 2000, where an IDENTICAL local edge flips ownership with the GLOBAL figure -- and no local rule can settle that. This covers the unambiguous case for free and leaves the ambiguous one to the flood that is actually buying something.
